I should probably let you in on a secret that's applicable to the vast majority of people.

Once you buy a project car, second car, or even your first car - you'll never have money again.

I've restored (or had restored) quite a few cars. One of the things I do, as mentioned, is upgrade the brakes - unless I'm leaving it stock. Like my 72 Dart is stock and has drums on all four corners.

The good news is that for your car, ~70 percent of the braking is done by the front wheels. (Some cars are modified to allow you to adjust the brake bias.) So, your front discs are doing the overwhelming majority of the work.

However, as I've stated before - including when I first started this sub, I'm a stickler for safety.

I really am.

Our hobby is dangerous. Our hobby is deadly. If you hit a solid object in your car at speed, you're hurt - badly. You're maybe even dead.

Being able to stop reliably and rapidly is a good thing. Drum brakes are damned near useless after a short spirited drive in the twisties. They build up so much heat that brake fade becomes a serious problem.

I'm not telling you what to do, but I'm SERIOUSLY recommending upgrading. If you hunt around at swap meets, you may well find a less expensive option.

Also, your car ABSOLUTELY has an owner's group/club. There's ABSOLUTELY a free online site/forum for your specific car. (I haven't looked, I'm just that certain.)

I'd SERIOUSLY recommend joining (with a different username, so you're not attached to your Voat ID) and asking questions, posting pics, etc... Get to know 'em and these types of communities are almost always awesome.

One of my favorite things about the automobile hobby is the community. It's seriously fucking awesome. I have a guy I can call about my 911, day or night, and he'll always take my call and help me. He asks for nothing in return, except maybe that you be as passionate as he is - or close. He's the kinda guy that knows every single piece on my model year and with my specific trim options.
